tagline: Asia's youngest nation, coffee and coral
overview:
Timor-Leste occupies the eastern half of the island of Timor, at the far southeastern end of the Indonesian archipelago and about 650 kilometers northwest of Australia. It also includes the enclave of Oecusse on the island's northern coast, surrounded by Indonesia, and two small islands. The whole country covers about 14,900 km², similar in size to Connecticut.

About 1.4 million people live here. Tetum and Portuguese are the official languages, and Indonesian and English are working languages, while more than fifteen local tongues are spoken in the mountains. Dili, the capital, lies on the northern coast beneath steep hills.

Timor-Leste is a parliamentary republic and one of the youngest countries in the world, fully independent since May 20, 2002. Offshore oil and gas have provided most government income, and the country is working to build farming, coffee exports and tourism as those reserves decline.
landAndNature: A rugged mountain spine runs the length of the country, rising to Tatamailau at 2,986 meters, so steep that road journeys of 100 kilometers can take many hours. The north coast is dry and hot with a short rainy season, while the south gets rain for much of the year. Coffee grows in the cool highlands under shade trees, much of it organic by default because farmers cannot afford chemicals. Eucalyptus and sandalwood, once the island's great export, cling to the slopes. The sea is the real treasure: the Ombai Strait off Atauro island has some of the highest reef fish diversity ever recorded, and blue whales, sperm whales and dolphins pass through the deep channel between the islands.
peopleAndCulture: Timorese society is built around clans and the uma lulik, a sacred house with a high thatched roof that holds a family's heirlooms and history. Weavings called tais, made on backstrap looms in patterns specific to each district, are given at weddings, funerals and welcomes. Most people are Catholic, a faith that became a symbol of identity during occupation, and village festivals mix church rituals with older ceremonies involving animal offerings and ancestor respect. Corn, rice, cassava and fish are everyday food, and coffee is drunk strong. Soccer is popular, along with a martial art dance called bidu. Tetum borrows many Portuguese words, so speakers slip between languages naturally.
history: Timor was famous for sandalwood, which drew Chinese and Malay traders centuries ago. Portugal claimed the east and the Dutch the west, dividing the island by treaty in 1859. Japan occupied Timor in World War II, and tens of thousands of Timorese died, many while helping Australian soldiers. Portugal withdrew in 1975, and days after Timor-Leste declared independence, Indonesia invaded. During 24 years of occupation an estimated 100,000 to 180,000 Timorese died from fighting, hunger and illness. In a United Nations referendum in 1999, nearly 80 percent voted for independence; violence followed, and much of the country was burned before international peacekeepers arrived. After a period of UN administration, Timor-Leste became fully independent on May 20, 2002. Two of its independence leaders, Bishop Belo and José Ramos-Horta, shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1996.
funFacts: Timor-Leste is called Timor Timur in Indonesian and Timór Lorosa'e in Tetum; both mean roughly 'east east'.
The country uses the US dollar as its currency but mints its own centavo coins.
Atauro island's reefs were found to have the highest average number of reef fish species of any surveyed site on Earth.
Nearly all Timorese coffee is grown without chemicals, mostly by smallholder families in shaded mountain gardens.
The giant statue of Cristo Rei above Dili stands atop a hill reached by climbing nearly 600 steps.
